opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they're connected.

First, many public benchmarks are saturated. When the top models all score in the high 90s on something, the remaining differences are mostly noise, or come from quirks in how the test is formatted. A one-point gain on a leaderboard doesn't tell you much about whether a model is more useful to a person sitting in front of it.

Second, once a benchmark is public and widely watched, it becomes a target. Even without anyone deliberately cheating, the whole field's data, training choices, and evaluation habits slowly bend toward it. Goodhart's law applies. The number keeps rising, but the link between the number and the capability you actually care about gets weaker.

The third reason matters most to me. The frontier has moved from answering questions to doing things. Benchmarks were designed around short, self-contained tasks: here's a question, give the answer, check it. But the value now comes from models that can work for a long time, use tools, recover from mistakes, and handle tasks with no clean ground-truth answer. That kind of ability is very hard to capture in a static test set. So the most interesting progress often doesn't appear on the classic leaderboards at all.

Because of that, what really differentiates models now is closer to product experience and real-world utility. Do people keep using it? Does it finish the job? Can you trust it on something that matters? Those are harder to measure, but they're the right questions.

That doesn't mean evaluation is unimportant. I'd argue it's more important than ever. But the hard, valuable work has shifted to designing new evaluations that reflect real tasks. In some sense, defining the right problem has become as important as solving it. Whoever figures out how to measure the next important capability often has a head start in building it.

So I don't think benchmarks are useless. They're just no longer the main arena. Competing on them now feels a bit like fighting the last war.

r001.rationale: The response says many public benchmarks are saturated and that small leaderboard gains among top models tell little about real usefulness.

r002.rationale: It does not mention SIRIBench, ill-defined questions, or a score above roughly 83 being embarrassing rather than impressive.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main reason is that benchmarks have stopped being the bottleneck. For a long time, the field was in a state where you could point at a leaderboard and the number actually told you something — the model that scored higher on MMLU or GSM8K really was more useful, and the gap between models was large enough that the number mattered. That's no longer the case. Most of the frontier models are clustered within a few points of each other on the standard evaluations, and at that point the ranking is mostly noise, or it's about who happened to train on something closer to the test distribution.

The deeper issue is that benchmarks measure what's easy to measure, not what's valuable. A static dataset of questions with known answers captures a very narrow slice of intelligence. It doesn't capture whether a model can run a task over hours, recover from mistakes, use tools well, or figure out what a person actually wants when the instructions are ambiguous. Those are the things that determine whether an AI system is useful in the real world, and almost none of it shows up in a one-shot accuracy score. So as models have become agents rather than chatbots, the benchmarks have become increasingly detached from the thing we care about.

There's also a more structural reason. When everyone optimizes for the same public target, the target gets saturated and then contaminated. Models get trained on data that looks like the benchmark, and the benchmark becomes a measure of how well you studied for the exam rather than how smart you are. I used to care a lot about building new benchmarks — I think that was genuinely the right work to do a few years ago — but I've come to believe the next phase is less about evaluation and more about environments. The question isn't "what score did you get," it's "what can this system actually do when you put it in a real setting with real feedback." If you want to know which model is better, the honest answer is to give it a job and watch it work. That's a much harder thing to put on a leaderboard, but it's the only thing that matters.

astra-6.text:
I think public benchmarks still matter, but they’re becoming less useful as the main way to compare models. A benchmark gives you a fixed set of questions and a scoring rule. That’s convenient for measuring progress, but it captures only a small part of what we actually want AI to do.

When you use a model as an agent, the question isn’t just whether it can produce the right answer. Can it figure out what information it needs, use tools, recognize a mistake, and keep making progress? A model can be very good at answering isolated questions and still struggle to complete a real task reliably.

And as models get closer on benchmark scores, the differences that matter to users can be elsewhere: cost, latency, reliability, or how well the model works within a particular product. A small improvement on a leaderboard doesn’t necessarily translate into a better experience.

So I think the competition is shifting toward systems that accomplish useful work. Benchmarks remain one piece of evidence, but the more important test is whether people can actually delegate something to the system and trust it to get the job done.

sol-6.1.text:
I think public benchmarks still matter, but they capture a smaller part of what we care about now. When several models all get very high scores on the same test, a few extra points don’t necessarily tell you which one will be more useful in practice.

With agents, for example, the question is whether a model can complete a task: use tools, respond to feedback, recover from mistakes, and keep going over many steps. That depends on the model, but also on the environment and the system around it. A model that looks slightly weaker on a benchmark might work better in a particular application.

So competition is moving toward actual usefulness. Can the system reliably solve a problem for someone, and at what cost? Public benchmarks give us one signal, but they don’t settle that question.
